newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Regret at Bass as UK blocks Carlsberg deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Regret at Bass as UK blocks Carlsberg deal.

text.p: Brewing giant Bass Plc responded with bitter disappointment on Friday as Britain blocked its merger with Carlsberg-Tetley, stating it was taken aback that the answer was such a "resounding no'.
Bass said in a statement it was "extremely disappointed",but pledged to continue to build its brewing business at home and abroad.
"It was a resounding 'no' and there's not a lot we can do about it," said a spokesman for the British group. "We don't know what caused Margaret Beckett to take that decision."

Margaret Beckett, the Labour government's new Trade and Industry Secretary, confounded expectations by announcing she was banning the deal rather than suggesting harsh conditions for clearance, as some analysts had been predicting earlier this week.

In her first major judgement on a competition issue since taking office last month, Beckett said in a statement that she agreed with the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC) that the deal would act against the public interest.
Bass shares reacted with initial gains before closing virtually unchanged, while Carlsberg shares fell.
Beckett said she disagreed with the MMC view that the negative effects of the mega-merger could be dealt with by demanding the sale of 1,900 Bass pubs.
"I am not persuaded that the divestment of 1,900 pubs would be an adequate counterweight to the substantial strengthening of Bass's position as a producer and wholesaler of beer," she said.

Beckett's decision to reject the deal marks a shift from past judgements on brewing mergers. Every acquisition in the beer industry since the Beer Orders Act of 1992 has required the merged group to reduce the size of its tied pub estate to gain clearance.

But Beckett said this deal would "represent a further substantial step in the direction of concentration of an industry which has already seen the number of national brewers with tied estates fall from six to four since 1989."
This referred to the British brewing industry's tied pub system whereby pubs can only sell beer brewed by their own company.

As part of her judgement Beckett has ordered Bass to divest itself of its 50 percent stake in Carlsberg-Tetley which it bought for 200 million pounds ($333.1 million) from Allied Domecq Plc under the terms of the merger sealed last August.

The deal would have made Bass Britain's biggest brewer, handing it 35 percent of the beer market. Its existing market share is 23 percent, below Scottish & Newcastle Plc which makes 29 pints out of every 100 consumed.
Bass told Reuters it was already in talks with competition watchdog the Office of Fair Trading on how to sell the stake.
Bass added that its net loss from the failed merger bid was around 60 million pounds before accounting for its own share of Carlsberg-Tetley profits, dividends and royalties.

Danish brewer Carlsberg confirmed it will buy back the stake for 110 million pounds. Ebbe Dinesen, Carlsberg-Tetley managing director said a "fundamental reorganisation" would be implemented in his company within the next few years.

Commenting on its own future, the Bass spokesman said, "We will continue to develop market share organically. We have strong brands and are one of the most cost-effective producers in the UK drinks sector."
Asked whether Bass would see job cuts from intensified cost-cutting now the merger had failed, he said, "From our point of view that is unlikely. But it could be a question for Carlsberg-Tetley."
British unions welcomed news of the merger's death, however. The T&G union said that had the deal gone ahead around 2,000 British jobs could have been lost.
When news of the merger block first hit the stock -market, the reaction was mixed. Bass surged ahead initially but ended the day flat at 735 pence per share.
Carlsberg shares were down sharply before recovering somewhat to end down 9.1 Danish crowns at 356.0 after a low of 344.0.

Analysts in London were mixed in their response to the Beckett announcement. Nick Lyle at SocGen said "I'm a bit taken aback. We had expected to see the deal to be tied to harsh conditions rather than completely blocked." But he said the financial cost of the failure was manageable for Bass.

Nigel Parson, analyst at Charterhouse Tilney, said the news was not so shocking when the political backdrop to the decision was considered. "It would have been very difficult for a new Labour government to consider a deal which would have led to job losses," he said.

Some market dealers also said Bass shares had reacted positively at first because as one player put it: "Carlsberg is not a great performer and people are saying it is a good thing Bass are out of it." ($ = 0.600 British Pounds)
